t.faya palaeolandscape@25.1,55.8:
Sharjah's interior is a world of red dunes, gravel plains and jagged limestone ridges, and in the middle of it, near the town of Mleiha, the hill of Jebel Faya holds one of the most important records of early human presence outside Africa. Excavations in rock shelters at the foot of the mountain have revealed stone tools spanning many tens of thousands of years, suggesting that early modern humans were present in Arabia far earlier than once thought, during periods when the climate was wetter and the desert greener. The Faya Palaeolandscape was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2025, recognising its significance for understanding human dispersal out of Africa.

Mleiha itself has a rich archaeological story, with Bronze Age and Iron Age tombs, and the remains of a pre-Islamic town that traded with the wider world. The Mleiha Archaeological Centre presents the finds and organises excursions into the desert, including to fossil sites and rock formations. The landscape is striking: the long ridge of Jebel Faya, the scattered acacia trees, and the dunes that glow orange in the late afternoon sun. At night the sky is dark, and the stars are brilliant.

The roads around Mleiha are excellent in the way that the UAE's roads usually are: wide, smooth and fast, with very little traffic away from the main highways. The road from Dhaid south toward Mleiha and on to the Hajar mountains passes through dunes and gravel plains, and the mountains to the east offer some great riding, with climbs and curves toward the east coast at Fujairah and Khor Fakkan. Watch out for sand on the road, especially after wind, and for camels, which wander freely. Summer heat is extreme, regularly over forty-five degrees, so the cooler months from November to March are the only sensible time to ride here.

Dhaid, about twenty-four kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size, with fuel stations, cafés and shops while Mleiha itself has only limited facilities. Bring plenty of water, because the desert can be dangerous in the heat, even in winter. Visit the centre first to understand the finds, then ride out to see the ridge, and watch the sunset over the dunes before heading back.
t.mission of santa ana@-16.6,-60.7:
Santa Ana is a tiny village in the lowlands of eastern Bolivia, in the Chiquitania region, and its church is considered by many to be the most authentic of the Jesuit missions of Chiquitos. The missions were founded by Jesuit priests in the late seventeenth and eighteenth centuries among the indigenous peoples of the region, the Chiquitanos, and became thriving communities centred on large churches built of wood and adobe, with vast roofs supported by carved wooden columns. Six of them were listed by UNESCO in 1990.

A Swiss Jesuit, Martin Schmid, played a key role in creating the architecture of the missions. An architect, musician and craftsman, he designed several of the churches and taught the local people to build instruments and play baroque music, which became central to mission life. The church at Santa Ana was built after the expulsion of the Jesuits in 1767, by the indigenous people themselves, following the same style, and it has kept much of its original character, with a simple wooden structure, a thatched or tiled roof and painted decoration. Its historic organ is still played, and the region hosts an international baroque music festival every two years, when concerts are held in the mission churches.

The landscape of the Chiquitania is a mix of dry forest, savannah, granite hills and cattle ranches, with red earth and big skies. The climate is hot, with a rainy season from about November to March, when tracks can become impassable, and a dry season from May to September, the best time to visit.

The riding here is an adventure. The main road from Santa Cruz to the missions is paved for much of its length, but the roads between villages are often unpaved, with red dust, sand and corrugations in the dry season and mud in the wet. Distances are long, traffic is light, and services are few. A dual-sport bike is best.

San Ignacio de Velasco, about thirty-seven kilometres away, is the main town of the region, with fuel, shops and accommodation; Concepción, a little closer, is smaller. Carry water and extra fuel. In the villages, simple restaurants serve rice, beef, chicken and cassava, and in the morning look for cuñapé, a cheese bread made with cassava flour. Sitting in the shade of the church in Santa Ana, listening to the birds and imagining the music that once filled the building, is a lovely way to spend an afternoon.
t.mission of san rafael@-16.8,-60.7:
The Jesuits who came to the lowlands of eastern Bolivia in the late seventeenth century did something remarkable with the forest, the heat and the people they found, the Chiquitano. Between 1691 and 1760 they founded a string of mission towns, and six of them survive, with churches built of wood and adobe, painted inside and out with floral patterns and trompe-l'oeil columns. San Rafael de Velasco, with its church finished in the 1740s, is one of the prettiest, a white and ochre building with a deep porch and an open bell tower, set in a village square with red earth and big shade trees. The missions were listed by UNESCO in 1990.

The man behind the architecture was a Swiss Jesuit, Martin Schmid, who was also a composer, and the missions were famous for their music. The Chiquitano learned to build violins, harps and organs, and to play baroque music of a surprisingly high standard, and manuscripts of that music were found in the archives. Every two years, an international festival of baroque music fills the churches with concerts, drawing musicians from many countries.

The Chiquitania is a place of dry forest, granite domes and open plains, east of Santa Cruz. The roads between the missions are a mix of paved highways and red dirt tracks, and while the main route from Santa Cruz to San Ignacio is paved and smooth, the side roads are not, and they turn to mud in the wet season, from November to March. May to October is the better time, though dust can be heavy, and nights can be cool.

I do not have a nearby town to name from the data, but San Ignacio de Velasco is the main centre of the area, with fuel, banks and hotels, and you should tank up there or in Santa Cruz before heading to the smaller missions. The villages have simple shops and a few places to eat, often serving grilled beef, rice with cheese and sweet cassava cakes. Take cash, as cards are rarely accepted, and leave plenty of time for dirt roads. The reward is the sight of a painted wooden church glowing in the evening light.
t.saigachy zhideyli@45.0,58.3:
Somewhere on the vast, empty Ustyurt plateau, between the Caspian and the dried-out Aral Sea, the map reads Saigachy-Zhideyli, and then it goes quiet. I do not know of a named monument at these coordinates, and there are no towns in my data within reach, so what follows is about the land itself. The Ustyurt is a high, flat desert of clay and limestone, cut at its edges by sheer white cliffs called chinks, and it lies partly in Kazakhstan and partly in Uzbekistan. It is one of the emptiest places in Eurasia.

The name gives the clue to the animal. The saiga is a small, odd-looking antelope with a swollen nose that filters dust and warms the air in winter, and herds of them once crossed these plateaux in huge numbers. Poaching and disease cut them to a tiny remnant by the early 2000s, and in 2015 a mass die-off killed more than half the world's saiga in Kazakhstan, but protection has helped, and the population has recovered a good deal in recent years. A rider might see a herd moving on the horizon, nervous and fast, or a lone wolf or a kulan, the wild ass.

The desert has a stark beauty. The sky is huge, the colours are subtle shades of ochre and grey, with sparse wormwood and saxaul scrub, and the silence is complete. In spring, tulips and other flowers carpet the clay for a few weeks, and in autumn the air is clear and the nights are cold. Summer is searingly hot, and winter brings blizzards and temperatures below minus twenty.

For travel, I must be blunt: this is expedition country. Roads, where they exist, are rough tracks of sand, gravel and broken asphalt, with no services for hundreds of kilometres, and navigation is by GPS. Fuel, water and food must be carried, and you should have recovery equipment, spares and a satellite communicator, and ideally travel with a second vehicle and local guides. Permits may be needed for border zones and reserves. In an emergency you may be a day or more from help.
t.saigachy@45.2,57.7:
Out on the plateau east of the Caspian, there are places where you can drive for a full day and meet nothing but sky. The Ustyurt, a vast, flat tableland of clay and limestone between the Caspian Sea and the Aral Sea basin, was the route of caravans for centuries, travelling between the oases of Khiva and the Mangyshlak coast, and old wells and graveyards still mark the way. The name Saigachy points to the antelope, but I do not know of any monument at these exact coordinates, and there are no towns nearby in my data, so I will speak about the region.

The plateau ends in steep cliffs, the chinks, which fall away several hundred metres to the dried-out bed of the Aral Sea. Once the fourth largest lake in the world, the Aral was drained from the 1960s when the rivers feeding it, the Amu Darya and Syr Darya, were diverted to irrigate cotton, and the fishing towns on its shores were left stranded in a salty desert. The scale of the disaster is hard to take in until you stand on the edge of the cliff and look down on the old sea floor, pale and cracked, with the odd rusty ship in the distance. In recent years, a dam in the northern part has helped to restore a small part of the lake.

On the plateau itself the wind is constant, and travellers should expect dust and cold. A rider should think carefully about safety, since roads are rare and often poor, and distances between settlements can be several hundred kilometres. Fuel, water and food must be carried, and the weather, from scorching summers to freezing winters with storms, can be severe. A satellite communicator and a local guide are wise precautions. The best seasons are spring and autumn.

Camels, wild asses and the occasional herd of saiga are the main life, along with eagles and larks, and the herders in their small settlements are hospitable, offering tea, bread and fermented camel milk, called shubat. Show respect, ask before photographing, and leave no rubbish behind.
t.old town lunenburg@44.4,-64.3:
Colour is the first thing that hits you in Lunenburg: wooden houses in mustard, barn red, teal and white, climbing the slope from the harbour in tidy rows. The town sits on Nova Scotia's South Shore, on a peninsula facing the Atlantic, and it is one of the best-preserved examples of a planned British colonial town in North America. It was founded in 1753, and the grid of streets laid out then is still the grid you walk now. The first settlers were largely Protestants from German-speaking lands, along with some Swiss and French, which is why you still hear names like Zwicker and Rhuland.

The harbour made the place. Lunenburg lived off the Grand Banks fishery, and its schooners and shipyards were famous. The most famous of all was the Bluenose, a racing and fishing schooner launched here in 1921, which won the international fishermen's trophy through the 1920s and 1930s and ended up on the Canadian dime. The Fisheries Museum of the Atlantic stands on the waterfront and tells that story, with vessels you can step aboard. Look up at the roofs too, because many of the houses have the so-called Lunenburg bump, a little dormer-like extension over the front door.

Getting here is a pleasure. The Lighthouse Route, Route 3, follows the coast through fishing coves and small harbours, with the sea on one side and spruce on the other, while Highway 103 is faster and quieter. Corners are gentle and roads are generally in decent shape, though frost heaves can bite in spring. Fog rolls in off the cold water, especially in early summer, and it can drop the temperature sharply, so carry a layer. September and early October are lovely, with warm days and cool nights, and the crowds thin out.

Lunenburg itself, with about 2,000 people, has cafés, pubs and small restaurants, and the steep streets are best walked rather than ridden. For fuel and a bigger supermarket, Bridgewater, about 17 km north, is the town to use. Seafood is the obvious thing to eat, from chowder to fresh scallops and lobster in season, and there is a smoked-fish and Solomon Gundy tradition in the area for the adventurous. Park near the waterfront and take an hour to wander uphill to the church on the hill, whose steeple stands out above the colourful roofs.
t.mission of san miguel@-16.7,-61.0:
Deep in the Bolivian lowlands, the Chiquitania is a land of dry tropical forest, red earth and granite outcrops, a long way from the Andes. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries Jesuit missionaries gathered the Chiquitano people into settlements here that blended European Baroque with local craft, and six of those mission towns survive. San Rafael and San Miguel, a short distance apart in the east, are among them, and UNESCO listed the group in 1990.

What you see is odd and wonderful. The churches look like they belong to a different continent, with wooden columns, painted facades and interiors covered in floral designs, but they were built by Indigenous craftsmen working with European designers. The architect and musician Martin Schmid, a Jesuit from Switzerland, designed several of the churches and composed music for the choirs. A manuscript tradition of Baroque music survives here, and a music festival in the missions draws players from many countries. San Rafael has especially fine painted decoration, much of it restored.

The ride is red-dust and heat. Roads across the Chiquitania run through open woodland, ranches and small villages, with stretches of fresh asphalt and stretches of gravel that become slick after rain. The rainy season runs roughly from November to March, and during it, dirt sections can become impassable. The dry season, from May to September, is the better time, but dust and heat are constant companions. Cattle and dogs wander onto the road, and trucks raise clouds.

Fuel is the thing to plan around. San Ignacio de Velasco, about thirty-seven kilometres away, is the largest town in the area and has fuel and hotels, while Concepcion, to the south, is another good stop. Smaller villages may have only informal fuel sold from drums, so top up when you can. Ordering a cold drink in the plaza, with the old church at your back and the dust settling, is one of the pleasures of this part of Bolivia. Allow a slow day, and leave time to walk inside.
t.saigachy duana@45.3,58.5:
There is nothing here with a name on a signpost, and that is the point. The coordinates fall on the Ustyurt plateau, the huge flat tableland of clay and limestone between the Caspian Sea and what remains of the Aral Sea, at the edge of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. The label comes from the saiga, the strange, bulbous-nosed antelope that has lived on these steppes since the days of mammoths, and the plateau's rim breaks away in cliffs, called chinks, that glow white, pink and ochre when the light is low.

The saiga story is one of the more hopeful ones in conservation. In the 1990s and 2000s poaching and disease cut the population to a tiny fraction of what it had been, and the animal was listed as critically endangered. Protection and a few lucky years brought a big rebound, especially in central Kazakhstan, although a mass die-off from bacterial infection in 2015 killed more than half of the world's saigas in a couple of weeks. It is a reminder that the animals here live on a knife edge. Seeing a herd moving over the plain, heads down and noses rippling, is the sort of luck you cannot plan.

Treat this as proper desert travel. Tracks across Ustyurt are mostly unsurfaced, can turn to sticky mud after rain and are marked by little more than other tyre tracks, so a GPS and a second source of navigation are not optional. The summers are fiercely hot, the winters bitter with wind, and spring and autumn are the best times, though even then nights are cold. There are no services for very long distances, so carry fuel, water and food, travel with another bike or vehicle, and tell somebody your plan. The nearest real supplies are in the towns of the surrounding regions, many hours away. Border zones in this part of Central Asia also need permits and attention to the rules.

If it goes well, the reward is the silence. The sky is huge, the horizon is very straight, and the only sounds are wind in dry grass and your own engine ticking as it cools. It will not be a day you forget.
t.jesuit missions of the chiquitos@-16.0,-:
The plains of eastern Bolivia look wholly unlike the Andes people picture. This is the Chiquitania, a gently rolling country of dry forest, red earth and granite outcrops, where in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries Jesuit priests founded a string of mission towns for the Chiquitano and other peoples. Six of the surviving churches are listed by UNESCO as the Jesuit Missions of Chiquitos, with San Francisco Javier, Concepción, Santa Ana, San Miguel, San Rafael and San José among them. They are working churches, and the wooden columns, painted ceilings and carved pulpits still serve their communities.

What makes them unusual is the blend. The Jesuits, among them the Swiss priest Martin Schmid, who built and designed several of the buildings, brought European forms and music, yet the craftsmen who built them were local, and the decoration shows it, with bright patterns that mix baroque and indigenous taste. Music was central, and today an international baroque festival grows from that heritage, which is a remarkable thing to find in the middle of cattle country. The missions were run as communal settlements until 1767, when the Spanish crown expelled the Jesuits from its territories.

For riders, the missions circuit is a long, gently rewarding journey. Paved roads link several of the main towns, and tracks join the others, with the surface changing quickly from smooth tarmac to rutted red dirt. The dry season, roughly May to October, is the sensible time, since the wet months make the clay roads slippery or impassable. Distances between fuel stops can be large, so top up whenever you pass a station in towns such as San Ignacio de Velasco or Concepción, and take extra water. Heat is a constant, and a siesta in the plaza under a tree is not laziness but good sense.

Evenings are the best time in the plazas, when families gather, children play in the dust, and the old churches glow in the setting sun. The food is simple and good, with beef, yuca and rice, and cold drinks are always welcome.
t.halifax@44.7,-63.6:
Halifax sits on one of the great natural harbours of the world, and most of its history is a story of that fact. The British founded the city in 1749 as a naval base to counter the French fortress at Louisbourg, and the star-shaped Citadel on the hill above the harbour is its monument, with a view across the water that explains the choice at once. Today it is the largest city in Atlantic Canada, with about 360,000 people in the municipality, and Dartmouth across the water adds another hundred thousand. A ferry has linked the two shores for more than two centuries, and a ride across costs very little and gives the best view of the skyline.

The city has seen its share of disaster. In December 1917 two ships collided in the narrows of the harbour, and one of them, loaded with explosives, blew up, devastating the north end of the city and killing nearly two thousand people. It remained the largest man-made explosion in history until the atomic bomb. Fairview cemetery holds the graves of many victims of the Titanic, whose bodies were brought here for burial. Pier 21, on the waterfront, was the arrival point for a million immigrants and is now a museum.

The riding begins outside town. The usual route to Grand Pré goes north-west on the 101, through the Annapolis Valley, a fertile strip of apple orchards, vineyards and farms between two ridges, then drops down to the Minas Basin, where the tides of the Bay of Fundy, among the highest in the world, rise and fall by more than ten metres. Grand Pré, a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, preserves the dykes and farmland made by the Acadians, who were deported by the British from here in 1755. The memorial church and statue are quiet and moving.

Halifax is well supplied with fuel, shops and restaurants. Try fresh lobster rolls, steamed mussels or the local oddity, the donair, a spiced beef wrap with a sweet sauce that is the city's official food. Weather is changeable, with sea fog rolling up the harbour in the morning, so carry a waterproof. Traffic through the downtown core and across the two harbour bridges can be heavy at rush hour, and some of the older streets are steep, so take it slowly. June to September is the most reliable season, and the Annapolis Valley is spectacular in blossom in late May.
t.dubai@25.2,55.3:
Dubai is a city that grew from a creek. For most of its history, it was a small trading and pearl-diving town on a tidal inlet, with merchants' houses behind wind towers, and the old quarters of Al Fahidi and Deira still show the low coral-and-gypsum buildings, with narrow lanes, where abras, the little wooden ferries, carry people across the water for a dirham or so. Then oil money and an extraordinary appetite for building transformed it, and today the skyline includes the Burj Khalifa, which at over 800 metres is the tallest structure ever built. The pin falls in the middle of the modern city.

The land around is desert, red-gold dunes, gravel plains and salt flats, and the contrast with the city is dramatic. Within an hour, you can be on a road with nothing but sand and the occasional camel. East of Sharjah lies the Faya palaeolandscape, a rocky area where archaeologists have found traces of some of the earliest human movements out of Africa, dating back around a hundred thousand years, and UNESCO listed it in 2023. The Hajar mountains rise to the east, bare and jagged, forming the border with Oman.

For riders, Dubai is a city of wide, fast roads. Sheikh Zayed Road and the other highways have many lanes, smooth tarmac and heavy traffic, and speed cameras are everywhere, with serious fines. The best riding is outside the city, on the Al Qudra desert road, the roads to Hatta in the hills and the long highway east. Sand drifts across the road at times, and camels sometimes wander near the edge. Summer heat is severe, with afternoon temperatures over forty-five degrees and humidity near the coast, so ride in the early morning or between November and March, when the days are mild and clear.

Practically, fuel is plentiful and relatively cheap, and there are stations on every main road. Food ranges from street shawarma to elegant restaurants, and bottled water is in every shop. Bring documents, because police checks are common, and make sure your licence and insurance cover riding in the UAE. Wear a full jacket, even when it looks too hot, because the wind dries you quickly. Stay hydrated, and plan your route to avoid the Friday afternoon jams.
t.sierra de la ventana@-38.1,-61.8:
The Sierra de la Ventana is a surprise in the middle of the pampas. After hundreds of kilometres of flat grassland, cattle and wind, the horizon in the south-west of Buenos Aires province lifts into a chain of folded quartzite ridges, the Sierras Australes, that rise to just over a thousand metres, grey and bare on top, and green with streams and groves of poplar below. The range is named for a natural window, the ventana, a gap in the crest of Cerro de la Ventana that frames the sky, and a steep path up the mountain leads to it for those who like walking.

Charles Darwin passed through in 1833 on his long journey across the pampas, and climbed to the ridge, and the account of his ascent is a point of local pride. In the valleys, the small town and nearby Villa Ventana grew up as a resort in the early twentieth century, when railway travel brought Buenos Aires families, and the style is that of a weekend retreat: stone and timber cottages, shady avenues, small guesthouses, a river for swimming and tea rooms with cakes. Most visitors come for the quiet, for walking and for the asado, the long Argentine barbecue.

A night here is a good way to break a long ride south-west from the capital. The roads leading in cross open grassland with huge skies, and wind is the main force, sometimes strong enough to push a bike sideways, so keep both hands on the bars and ride steadily. The approach roads are long and straight, but within the hills the lanes wind gently along streams, with tight bends and unpaved sections on some of the side roads. Watch for cattle on the road and for trucks on the main route.

Fuel is the thing to plan. The village has a station, but supplies can run out, so fill up when you can in Tornquist or Saldungaray on the way. Weather is variable, with cool nights even in summer, and snow possible on the highest ridges in winter. The best seasons are spring and autumn, when the days are mild and the hills green or golden.
t.cerro ventana view@-38.1,-61.9:
The Pampas are famously flat, which is why the Sierra de la Ventana looks so improbable, a long wall of quartzite ridges erupting from the grassland in the south of Buenos Aires province. Cerro de la Ventana is the one with the hole in it. Near the crest, at a little over a thousand metres, erosion has punched a natural window through the rock, and on a clear day from the plain you can see the sky through it like a small bright coin. The trail to it takes a few hours of steady uphill walking, and it is a rite of passage for people from Bahía Blanca and the capital.

Charles Darwin climbed one of these hills in 1833 during the Beagle's voyage, and wrote about the odd contrast of the rough quartz crags with the endless plain around them. The ranges here, the Sierras Australes, are among the oldest in Argentina, and their rock was folded and worn down hundreds of millions of years ago. The air is dry and clean, the light on the ridges in the late afternoon is a copper colour, and the grass around the foothills smells of thyme and dust.

For a rider coming from the flat country, the first thing to notice is the wind. It blows steadily across the plain, and it can lean a bike over on the long straight roads that lead to the hills. Routes 76 and 72 run through small farming towns, with gravel side roads that wander toward the sierra, and the sealed roads are generally quiet. Cattle and horses graze beside the fences, and occasionally a rhea runs along the verge. Gravel surfaces can be loose and unforgiving, so take care and keep the speed down.

The town of Sierra de la Ventana, a short distance east, is the base for visitors, with cabins, a few restaurants, a bakery and a station on the old railway. The best seasons are spring and autumn, when the days are mild and the grass is green. Summer afternoons can be hot, and winter brings frost and sometimes snow on the peaks.

Argentine meat is the obvious lunch, and a roadside parrilla with a plate of beef and a glass of red is a fine way to finish the day.
t.tornquist hills@-38.1,-62.2:
West of the Cerro de la Ventana, the hills crowd in around the town of Tornquist and its provincial park, and the country becomes more rugged and more varied. Ernesto Tornquist, a banker and landowner of the late nineteenth century, owned these lands, and the park that bears his name protects a stretch of the Sierras Australes with some of the best walking in the province. Cerro Tres Picos, the highest summit in Buenos Aires province at about 1,239 metres, is nearby, and the surrounding hills carry names like Napostá Grande and Bonete.

These ranges hold something special for a flat country. In the folds, there are small streams, waterfalls and patches of native shrubs, and the grassland contains plants found nowhere else. Guanacos, foxes and the armadillos called pichis are present, along with the occasional puma, rarely seen. Birds are plentiful, with caracaras, falcons and, in the right season, flocks of parakeets. The hills are dry for much of the year, but after rain, the streams run clear and the slopes turn green.

Riding here means long approaches across a plain that seems to go on forever, and then a sudden rise of rock and a twist in the road. Route 76 runs between Tornquist and Sierra de la Ventana, a good road with a few gentle curves, and unpaved tracks lead off into the hills and the park. The unpaved roads, called ripio, are loose and need care, particularly on a heavy bike, and a day of rain makes them slick. The wind is fierce at times, and in spring it carries a fine dust, so goggles are a help.

Tornquist is a quiet farming town of a few thousand people, with fuel stations, shops and a couple of simple restaurants. It has the sort of calm, tree-lined feeling typical of Argentine country towns, with a plaza and a church, and a mate gourd is passed around in the evening. The town grew up around the railway, which brought wheat and cattle to the port at Bahía Blanca, and the old station is still a landmark.

Fill the tank in town, and carry water if you plan on exploring. The distances are bigger than they look, and the next services can be an hour away.
t.tarabuco@-19.2,-64.9:
Come on a Sunday or do not bother, is the local wisdom, because Tarabuco is a small highland town with a very large market once a week. It sits in the hills east of Sucre at around 3,300 metres, roughly forty kilometres from the city, and it belongs to the Yampara people, whose weaving traditions are among the finest in Bolivia. The streets are quiet most days and then fill on Sunday morning with farmers, weavers and buyers from the surrounding valleys.

The textiles are the draw. Look for the dense, geometric patterns woven in dark red, black and cream, often showing animals, crops and village scenes, and for the men's costumes, which include a leather helmet-like hat called a montera, based on the headgear of the Spanish conquistadors. People wear these every day, not for show. If you want to buy, bargain with a smile and do not rush; the best pieces take months of work and the price reflects it.

History lives in the town as well. In 1816 a Yampara and mestizo force fought Spanish troops in the Battle of Jumbate nearby, and the event is remembered each March in the Pujllay festival, with music, dancing, chicha and a good deal of noise. If you are riding the region at that time, the whole area turns festive, and you might find rooms booked out.

The road in from Sucre climbs out of the valley through a dry, folded landscape of red earth, terraced fields, and eucalyptus stands, with views that open wide on the ridges. It is a rewarding ride for the changes of scenery more than outright speed. Take it in the morning, before the market begins to crowd the last stretch and when the light is clear on the hills. Watch for animals, farm vehicles and people on the road, especially on market day, and slow down when you enter the village.

Tarabuco is small, with a population of about two and a half thousand, so do not rely on it for fuel; fill up in Sucre before you leave, where there are plenty of stations. Cafés and market stalls provide hearty soup, grilled meat, and cups of hot tea, which are welcome in the cool air. Carry something warm even on a bright day.
t.wadi wurayah@25.5,56.3:
Wadi Wurayah lies in the Hajar mountains on the east coast of the Emirates, in the narrow strip of Fujairah that reaches the Gulf of Oman, and it is one of the few places in the country where water stays on the surface all year. A stream runs through the gorge, feeding pools and small falls beneath tall, folded cliffs of limestone and ophiolite, rock that was once part of the ocean floor and was pushed up onto the land when plates collided. It was the first mountain protected area in the Emirates and is now a national park. Fish live in the pools, and the rarer animals include the Arabian tahr, a shy mountain goat that few visitors ever see.

The region around is dry, jagged and handsome, with grey and rusty slopes, wild acacia, date palms in the villages and the sea just beyond. The villages of Dibba, split between three jurisdictions, Fujairah, Sharjah and Oman's Musandam, sit by a wide bay beneath the peaks. The towns on this coast have a fishing and farming past that feels very different from the glass cities of Dubai, and the Friday market in the area is a good place to buy fruit and dates.

On a motorcycle the approach is a pleasure. Roads over the mountains from Sharjah and Dubai have fast, open curves and good surface, with long views over the barren ridges, and the coast road leads north and south from Dibba with the sea on one side and the mountains on the other. Traffic is light on weekdays, and heavier at weekends when families drive across for the beach. The summer heat is fierce, with humid air on the coast, so the cooler months from November to March are far better, and rain can bring flash floods in the wadis, so never ride or park in a dry channel when clouds are on the peaks.

Dibba Al-Fujairah is about twelve kilometres away and has fuel, shops and cafes, and the bigger towns of Khor Fakkan and Fujairah are not much farther. Bring water with you, since the reserve itself has few facilities and access may be limited by the authorities, so check before you go. Sunrise on the coast, with the mountains turning pink, is a fine reward for an early start.

t.halifax@44.6,-63.6:
Halifax sits on one of the great natural harbours of the world, and most of its history is a story of that fact. The British founded the city in 1749 as a naval base to counter the French fortress at Louisbourg, and the star-shaped Citadel on the hill above the harbour is its monument, with a view across the water that explains the choice at once. Today it is the largest city in Atlantic Canada, with about 360,000 people in the municipality, and Dartmouth across the water adds another hundred thousand. A ferry has linked the two shores for more than two centuries, and a ride across costs very little and gives the best view of the skyline.

The city has seen its share of disaster. In December 1917 two ships collided in the narrows of the harbour, and one of them, loaded with explosives, blew up, devastating the north end of the city and killing nearly two thousand people. It remained the largest man-made explosion in history until the atomic bomb. Fairview cemetery holds the graves of many victims of the Titanic, whose bodies were brought here for burial. Pier 21, on the waterfront, was the arrival point for a million immigrants and is now a museum.

The riding begins outside town. The usual route to Grand Pré goes north-west on the 101, through the Annapolis Valley, a fertile strip of apple orchards, vineyards and farms between two ridges, then drops down to the Minas Basin, where the tides of the Bay of Fundy, among the highest in the world, rise and fall by more than ten metres. Grand Pré, a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, preserves the dykes and farmland made by the Acadians, who were deported by the British from here in 1755. The memorial church and statue are quiet and moving.

Halifax is well supplied with fuel, shops and restaurants. Try fresh lobster rolls, steamed mussels or the local oddity, the donair, a spiced beef wrap with a sweet sauce that is the city's official food. Weather is changeable, with sea fog rolling up the harbour in the morning, so carry a waterproof. Traffic through the downtown core and across the two harbour bridges can be heavy at rush hour, and some of the older streets are steep, so take it slowly. June to September is the most reliable season, and the Annapolis Valley is spectacular in blossom in late May.
